stem: A 30-year-old woman with blood group AB is scheduled for elective surgery. Which of the following best explains why she can receive packed red cells from donors of any ABO group?

options.label: A
options.text: Her erythrocytes lack A and B antigens entirely
options.misconception: Group O red-cell phenotype is being ascribed to group AB.
options.explanation: Group AB erythrocytes express both A and B antigens; what she lacks are anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma.

options.label: B
options.text: Her plasma lacks preformed anti-A and anti-B antibodies
options.misconception: None; without anti-A/B she does not agglutinate donor A, B, or O red cells.
options.explanation: AB recipients have A and B antigens on their own red cells and therefore do not make anti-A or anti-B; donor red cells of any ABO group are not attacked by her plasma.

options.label: C
options.text: Her plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
options.misconception: The group O plasma pattern is being applied to group AB.
options.explanation: Anti-A and anti-B define group O plasma (universal plasma donor risk to recipients); AB plasma lacks those antibodies.

options.label: D
options.text: Her Rh status alone determines ABO compatibility
options.misconception: Rh and ABO systems are being conflated.
options.explanation: Rh compatibility is separate; ABO compatibility for red cells depends on whether recipient plasma has anti-A/B against donor antigens.

options.label: E
options.text: Her hepatocytes clear incompatible antigen before agglutination
options.misconception: A clearance mechanism is being invented to replace antibody absence.
options.explanation: ABO incompatibility is antibody-mediated agglutination/hemolysis; AB recipients are safe for any ABO red cells because they lack anti-A/B.

context: Learning objective: distinguish universal red-cell donor (O) from universal red-cell recipient (AB). AB plasma lacks anti-A and anti-B, so any ABO donor red cells are accepted.
